title: Why Does Alcohol Make You Emotional? Angry, Happy, or Crying
excerpt: Why alcohol makes some people angry, others happy, and others cry. The brain science behind drunk emotions, why it varies, the next-day mood dip, and how to stay steadier.
metaDescription: Why does alcohol make you angry, happy, or teary? The brain science behind drunk emotions, the next-day mood dip, and how to keep your mood steadier.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: why does alcohol make me angry
content:
**The answer first:** alcohol makes you emotional because it quiets the parts of your brain that normally hold your feelings in check, while turning up the volume on whatever you were already feeling. It dampens the prefrontal cortex, the area behind your forehead that plans, weighs consequences, and puts the brakes on impulses. At the same time it boosts feel-good chemicals early in the night and narrows your attention to whatever is right in front of you. The result is that a small mood becomes a big one. If you came in relaxed and among friends, you get happy and warm. If you came in stressed, hurt, or tired, the same drinks can tip you into anger or tears.

**The quick version of what helps:** pace yourself (roughly one drink an hour or slower), eat beforehand, alternate with water, and notice your mood before the first drink. If you already feel raw, angry, or low, that's the night to drink less or not at all. Avoid big conversations, arguments, and texts after several drinks, because your brain is literally less able to see the long-term consequences. And expect some emotional fallout the next day, since the rebound from alcohol can leave you anxious or flat.

> **When to see a doctor or get help.** Getting a bit teary or snappy after a few drinks is common and usually not a sign of anything serious. But talk to a doctor if your mood after drinking is regularly frightening to you or the people around you, if you become aggressive or violent when you drink, if you often can't remember what you said or did, or if low mood, anxiety, or irritability lasts for days after drinking. If you shake, sweat, feel your heart racing, or feel deeply anxious whenever you go a day without alcohol, those can be signs of physical dependence, and a doctor can help you stop safely. **If you have thoughts of hurting yourself or someone else, get help now:** in the US, call or text **988** (Suicide and Crisis Lifeline), or call **911** in an emergency. Outside the US, contact your local emergency number.

## How Alcohol Changes Your Emotions: The Brain Science in Plain Words

Alcohol isn't a single switch in the brain. It nudges several systems at once, and the mix of effects is what makes drunk emotions so unpredictable.

**1. It slows down your brain's brakes.** Alcohol boosts the activity of GABA, the brain's main calming messenger, and blocks glutamate, its main "go" messenger. That combination slows nerve signaling in general. (We cover this in more detail in our guide to [alcohol and GABA](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-gaba).) The prefrontal cortex is especially sensitive to this slowdown. This is the part of the brain that holds an impulse in check while you think, "Is this a good idea?" When it is dulled, feelings travel more directly into words and actions.

**2. It releases feel-good chemicals at first.** Drinking triggers a release of dopamine and the brain's own opioids (endorphins) in reward areas. A well-known 2012 brain-imaging study published in *Science Translational Medicine* (Mitchell and colleagues) found that alcohol caused endorphin release in reward-related regions, and that heavier drinkers felt more pleasure from that release. This is a big part of why the first drink or two feel warm and lifting.

**3. It narrows your attention.** Psychologists Claude Steele and Robert Josephs described this in 1990 as "alcohol myopia," meaning drunk nearsightedness. Alcohol reduces how much information your brain can process at once, so you focus on whatever is most obvious in the moment and lose track of the background. If the most obvious thing is a funny friend and a great song, you're delighted. If it's a rude comment or a painful memory, that becomes your whole world.

**4. It changes how you read threats and faces.** Research on alcohol and the amygdala, the brain's alarm center, suggests alcohol can blunt your reaction to some threats while also making you worse at reading other people's expressions accurately. A neutral face can look hostile. A joke can land as an insult. Combined with weaker brakes, that is fertile ground for conflict.

**5. It wears off unevenly.** As your blood alcohol level falls, the brain tries to rebalance. The calming effect fades and the system can swing the other way, toward restlessness and anxiety. That is why the same night can go from euphoric to grumpy to weepy, and why the next morning often brings a wave of worry.

None of these effects create emotions out of nothing. They amplify, release, and distort what's already there. That's the single most useful idea for understanding your own drunk moods.

## Why Does Alcohol Make Me Angry?

Anger is the most-searched version of this question, and the most important one to understand, because alcohol-related anger can damage relationships and lead to real harm.

Researchers have studied the link between alcohol and aggression for decades. A classic review by Bushman and Cooper in *Psychological Bulletin* (1990) pulled together experimental studies and concluded that alcohol does increase aggressive behavior, particularly when people are provoked. That last part matters. Alcohol doesn't usually make calm people pick fights out of nowhere. It makes people react more strongly when something annoys them.

Here's why that happens:

- **Weaker impulse control.** Brain-imaging research on alcohol and aggression has found reduced activity in the prefrontal areas that normally regulate an angry response. The anger signal comes through, but the "wait, don't" signal is muted.
- **Misreading other people.** With alcohol myopia, you notice the provocation (a bump at the bar, a sarcastic tone) and miss the context (it was an accident, they were joking). You react to the narrowest, most obvious interpretation.
- **Lower worry about consequences.** Sober, the thought of losing a friendship or getting into trouble holds you back. Drunk, those future costs feel distant and abstract. Researchers have found that people who tend to focus on the present rather than the future are more prone to alcohol-related aggression, which fits this picture.
- **Physical discomfort.** Being hot, crowded, tired, hungry, or dehydrated all make irritability more likely, and nights out tend to stack all of them together.
- **The rebound.** Late in the evening, as alcohol levels drop, many people get irritable and short-tempered. If you notice you get snappy "at the end of the night," this is likely why.

Some people are clearly more prone to this than others. Personal temperament, how much stress you're carrying, family patterns, and whether you've learned to associate drinking with conflict all play a role. If you've been told more than once that you become a different, angrier person when you drink, treat that as useful information rather than an accusation.

**What actually helps with angry drinking:**

1. **Drink less per session.** The aggression effect gets stronger with higher doses. Stopping at one or two drinks keeps the prefrontal brakes more intact.
2. **Don't drink when you're already angry.** Using alcohol to "calm down" after a fight or a bad day often backfires because it amplifies the mood you bring to it.
3. **Avoid known triggers.** If certain people, topics, or venues set you off, skip them on drinking nights.
4. **Have an exit rule.** Decide in advance: "If I feel my temper rising, I go outside, get water, and leave." It's much easier to follow a rule you set sober.
5. **No serious talks after drinking.** Postpone money talks, relationship conflicts, and anything that already feels tense until you're sober.

If drinking has led to you hurting someone, damaging property, or scaring people you love, please talk to a doctor or counselor. That's not a character judgment. It's a pattern that responds well to help.

## Why Does Alcohol Make Me Cry?

Crying when drunk is extremely common, and it often surprises people who don't consider themselves emotional. There are a few overlapping reasons.

**Feelings you've been holding back come out.** Most of us spend the day managing our emotions without noticing. We push down sadness at work, stay composed after bad news, and put on a brave face. Alcohol weakens that management system. Sadness that was being held in check suddenly has a direct path out.

**Narrowed attention locks onto the sad thing.** If you start thinking about a breakup, a loss, or a worry while drinking, alcohol myopia makes it hard to shift away. You can end up circling the same painful thought, which deepens the feeling.

**The comedown phase.** The early lift from dopamine and endorphins fades within a couple of hours, and the brain's rebound can feel like a dip in mood. Many people describe a pleasant first hour followed by a sad or lonely second half of the night.

**Tiredness.** Alcohol is sedating, and nights out tend to run late. Being exhausted on its own makes people tearful. Add alcohol and the effect is bigger.

**Music, nostalgia, and people.** Drinking often happens in settings designed to stir feelings: weddings, reunions, farewells, sad songs at 1 a.m. Alcohol makes those feelings hit harder.

Crying after drinking isn't a problem in itself. Sometimes it's even a release that people feel better for. What's worth paying attention to is whether it's frequent, whether the same painful subject comes up every time, and whether you feel low long after the alcohol has worn off. Alcohol is a depressant of the nervous system (see our explainer on [whether alcohol is a depressant](/never-hungover/is-alcohol-a-depressant)), and regular heavy drinking is linked to worse mood over time. If drinking keeps bringing up the same grief or sadness, that's often a sign the feeling needs attention when you're sober, with a friend, therapist, or doctor. Our article on [alcohol and depression](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-depression) goes deeper on that link.

## Why Does Alcohol Make Me Happy?

The happy, chatty, affectionate drunk is the effect most people are hoping for, and it has a clear biological basis.

- **Reward chemicals.** The early release of dopamine and endorphins produces a genuine lift in mood and a sense of warmth.
- **Lower social anxiety.** By calming the nervous system and reducing worry about what others think, alcohol makes many people feel more relaxed and outgoing.
- **Attention on the good stuff.** In a fun setting, alcohol myopia keeps your focus on the jokes and music, and your everyday worries fade into the background.
- **Expectations.** What you expect alcohol to do shapes how you feel. Studies using placebo drinks have shown that people who believe they're drinking alcohol often act more relaxed and sociable even when there's little or none in the glass. Context and expectation do a lot of the work.

This happy phase usually sits at the lower end of drinking: the first one or two drinks for most people. Beyond that, the sedating and impairing effects start to outweigh the lift. People often chase the feeling of the first hour with more drinks, but the extra alcohol tends to bring tiredness, sloppiness, and mood dips rather than more happiness. That's worth knowing if you want to keep the good part of the night.

## Why Does Alcohol Make Some People Sad and Others Happy?

Two people can drink the same amount and have very different emotional nights. The main reasons:

**Your mood going in.** This is the biggest factor. Alcohol is an amplifier. Stressed in, more stressed out. Content in, more content out.

**Your setting.** A relaxed dinner with friends and a tense family gathering produce very different drunk moods from the same drink.

**Your expectations and history.** If drinking has always been tied to celebration for you, you'll lean that way. If it's been tied to conflict or coping, that pattern can show up too.

**Your personality.** In a 2017 study in *Clinical Psychological Science*, Winograd and colleagues asked whether people really become different people when drunk. Participants reported changes across several personality traits, with the biggest being a rise in extraversion. Interestingly, outside observers noticed fewer changes than the drinkers themselves reported. In other words, you may feel like a very different person, but to others you may look like a louder version of yourself.

**Your body.** Body size, sex, how fast you drank, whether you ate, and how quickly your body clears alcohol all change how high your blood alcohol level gets. A faster rise generally means stronger effects in both directions.

**Your sleep and stress.** Being run down, sleep-deprived, or under pressure all lower your emotional reserves before the first drink.

## Why Do I Feel Emotional the Day After Drinking?

Plenty of people feel fine while drinking and then wake up anxious, guilty, tearful, or irritable. This is often called "hangxiety," and it's common enough that we've written a full [guide to hangxiety](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research).

Several things contribute:

- **The rebound effect.** While you drink, your brain adapts to alcohol's calming effect. When the alcohol is gone, the brain is left temporarily tilted toward excitability, which shows up as restlessness, jumpiness, and worry.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol may help you fall asleep, but it disrupts sleep later in the night, especially the dreaming stage. A short, broken night leaves anyone more emotional. If this is a pattern for you, our article on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's going on.
- **Physical hangover symptoms.** Headache, nausea, low blood sugar, and dehydration make it hard to feel emotionally steady.
- **Memory gaps and worry.** Not remembering exactly what you said can fuel anxiety. If you regularly lose chunks of the night, that's worth taking seriously (see our page on [blackouts](/never-hungover/blackout-drunk)).
- **Real regrets.** Sometimes the emotional hangover is pointing at something real, like an argument or a message you wish you hadn't sent. Dealing with it directly, once you're sober, usually helps more than replaying it.

For most social drinkers, this next-day mood dip passes within a day. Hydrating, eating a proper meal, getting outside, and an early night all help. If low mood or anxiety regularly lasts several days after drinking, mention it to a doctor.

## Why Does Alcohol Make Me Say Things I Don't Mean (or Do Mean)?

People often say "drunk words are sober thoughts." That's only partly true.

Alcohol does lower your filter, so thoughts you'd normally keep to yourself are more likely to come out. Sometimes those are real feelings you've been holding back. But alcohol also distorts what you're feeling in the moment. Narrowed attention can blow a minor irritation out of proportion. Misread facial expressions can make you think someone is angry with you when they aren't. And the emotional amplification means that a passing thought can come out with far more force than you'd ever mean.

So a drunk statement is better understood as "an exaggerated version of a passing feeling" than "the hidden truth." If someone said something hurtful while drinking, it's reasonable to talk about it when you're both sober, without assuming the drunk version was the whole story. And if you're the one who tends to blurt things out, a simple rule helps: no texts, posts, or serious conversations after the second drink.

## Is Getting Emotional When Drinking a Sign of a Problem?

Usually not. For most people, occasional happy, teary, or irritable moments while drinking are a normal response to a drug that alters brain chemistry.

It's worth taking a closer look if:

- You often get angry, aggressive, or frightening to others when you drink.
- You drink specifically to manage feelings like stress, sadness, or loneliness, and need more to get the same effect.
- Drinking regularly brings up the same painful subject.
- You often don't remember parts of the night.
- Your low mood or anxiety after drinking lasts for days.
- People close to you have raised concerns.

None of these mean anything dramatic about you. They are signs that alcohol is doing more emotional work in your life than you'd probably like, and a conversation with a doctor is a reasonable next step. Many people find that simply cutting back on the amount per session makes a big difference to how they feel during and after.

One more practical point: alcohol mixes badly with many medicines that affect mood, including some antidepressants, anti-anxiety medicines, and sleep aids. If you take any of these and notice big emotional swings when you drink, talk to your prescriber. Our article on [antidepressants and alcohol](/never-hungover/antidepressants-and-alcohol) covers the most common combinations.

## How to Keep Your Emotions Steadier When You Drink

The most reliable tools are simple, and they all work by keeping your blood alcohol level lower and steadier:

1. **Check your mood first.** Ask yourself honestly how you feel before the first drink. If you're upset, exhausted, or angry, plan to drink less or skip it.
2. **Eat before and while drinking.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which smooths out the highs and dips.
3. **Pace yourself.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour (it varies from person to person). Drinking faster than that steadily raises your level and the emotional effects.
4. **Alternate with water.** It slows your pace and helps with next-day symptoms.
5. **Set a limit in advance.** Decide your number before you start, when your judgment is fully intact.
6. **Choose your company and setting.** Supportive people and relaxed settings make a good drunk mood more likely.
7. **Protect your sleep.** Stop drinking a few hours before bed so your sleep is less disrupted, which helps your mood the next day.
8. **Have a plan for big feelings.** If you notice anger or sadness building, step outside, get water, call it a night, and save the conversation for tomorrow.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the pacing and hydration habits with the best evidence, which also happen to be the habits that keep your mood steadiest.

## Where Does DHM Fit In?

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that some people take when they drink. It's relevant to this topic because of how it was first studied: a 2012 study in rats published in *The Journal of Neuroscience* (Shen and colleagues) found that DHM acted on the same GABA receptors that alcohol affects and reduced several signs of intoxication and withdrawal in the animals.

That's interesting research, but it's important to be clear about its limits. Those results come from animals. There is no good evidence that DHM changes how emotional you get while drinking in people, and it does not prevent anger, aggression, or poor judgment. It's not a reason to drink more, and it doesn't replace pacing, eating, and knowing your limits. Some people use it alongside those habits mainly for next-day comfort.

If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when. If you take any medication, especially for mood, anxiety, or sleep, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

Alcohol makes you emotional because it weakens your brain's self-control system, gives you a short burst of feel-good chemicals, narrows your attention to whatever is in front of you, and then rebounds as it wears off. It doesn't invent feelings. It amplifies and distorts the ones you already have. That's why the same drinks can make you happy one night, angry the next, and teary the one after.

The practical takeaways are straightforward. Pay attention to your mood before you drink. Keep your intake low and slow. Avoid serious conversations and messages after a few drinks. Expect some next-day emotional wobble and treat it kindly. And if drinking regularly brings out anger, deep sadness, or memory gaps, talk to a doctor. That's a sensible step, not an overreaction.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does alcohol make me angry?**

Alcohol dulls the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain that holds impulses in check, and narrows your attention to whatever is most obvious in the moment. So when something annoys you, you react more strongly and think less about the consequences. Research on alcohol and aggression shows the effect is strongest when people feel provoked. Being tired, hot, hungry, or already stressed makes it more likely, and irritability often rises late in the night as alcohol levels fall.

**Why do I cry when I drink?**

Alcohol weakens the mental effort you normally use to keep sadness in check, so feelings you've been holding back come out more easily. It also narrows your focus, which can lock you onto a painful thought, and the early mood lift fades into a dip within a couple of hours. Tiredness and emotional settings like weddings or farewells add to it. Occasional drunk crying is common; frequent crying about the same subject is worth talking through when you're sober.

**Why does alcohol make me happy at first and then sad?**

The first drink or two release dopamine and the brain's own endorphins, which lift your mood and ease social anxiety. As your blood alcohol rises further, alcohol's sedating effects take over, and as it starts to fall, the brain rebounds toward restlessness and low mood. That's why many people feel great in the first hour and flat, teary, or irritable later in the night.

**Do drunk people say what they really mean?**

Partly. Alcohol lowers your filter, so thoughts you'd normally keep private are more likely to come out. But it also exaggerates and distorts feelings, so a passing irritation can come out sounding like a deep conviction. A drunk statement is best treated as an exaggerated version of a real feeling, and it's worth discussing calmly once everyone is sober.

**Why do I feel anxious or emotional the day after drinking?**

As alcohol leaves your system, your brain is temporarily tilted toward excitability after adapting to alcohol's calming effect. Add poor sleep, dehydration, low blood sugar, and worry about what you said or did, and many people feel anxious, guilty, or tearful the next day. This usually passes within a day. If it regularly lasts several days, mention it to a doctor.

**Is getting emotional when drinking a sign of a drinking problem?**

Not by itself. Feeling happier, teary, or snappier after a few drinks is a normal response to how alcohol affects the brain. It's worth talking to a doctor if you often become aggressive, regularly drink to manage your feelings, frequently lose memory of the night, or feel low for days afterward. If you shake, sweat, or feel very anxious whenever you skip a day of drinking, a doctor can help you stop safely.

**How can I avoid getting emotional when I drink?**

Check your mood before drinking and drink less (or not at all) if you're already upset or exhausted. Eat first, pace yourself at about one drink an hour or slower, alternate with water, and set a limit in advance. Avoid serious conversations and texting after a few drinks, and step away if you feel anger or sadness building.

**Can DHM stop alcohol from making me emotional?**

There is no good evidence that DHM changes how emotional you get while drinking in people. Early research in rats found DHM acts on the same GABA receptors alcohol affects, but human data is limited. DHM doesn't prevent anger or poor judgment and isn't a reason to drink more. Pacing, eating, and keeping your intake low are what keep your mood steadier.
